How do Weekly Thing and Thingy connect?

things.body:
The Weekly Thing is my newsletter of links I found interesting, each with my commentary, plus my own blog posts from the week. I sent the [first issue](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/1/) on May 13, 2017, and have sent it most weekends since, taking breaks in summer and over the winter holidays. It began on TinyLetter, moved to MailChimp with [issue 23](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/23/) in October 2017, and moved to Buttondown with [issue 131](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/131/) in January 2020. I numbered those moves myself: “1.0: Launch on TinyLetter, 2.0: Move to MailChimp, 2.1: Custom HTML Template, 3.0: Buttondown.” I reached [issue 100](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/100/) in April 2019, [200](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/200/) in October 2021, and [300](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/300/) in November 2024, which took “7 years 5 months 3 weeks and 6 days” ([Thoughts after writing 300 newsletters](https://www.thingelstad.com/2024/11/17/thoughts-after-writing.html)).

In May 2026, at 345 issues, I [rebuilt the website](https://www.thingelstad.com/2026/05/07/massive-weekly-thing-website-build.html) as a full archive with search, a table of contents for each issue, and Thingy for asking questions of the archive. The ten newest issues also got an audio edition, published as a [podcast](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/podcast/). I built it with Claude Code, Claude Design, and Codex. [Issue 349](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/349/), two weeks later, was the first made in the Weekly Thing Workshop, a team of Discord agents. Starting with [issue 350](https://www.thingelstad.com/2026/09/20/i-just-published-weekly-thing.html) in September 2026, every issue has been written and sent from WT Builder. In October 2026 I [restructured the whole archive](https://www.thingelstad.com/2026/10/06/weekly-thing-archive-improved.html) so old issues render like new ones, and rendered every issue in audio, so the podcast feed “goes all the way back to the very first issue.”

Readers have had places to talk about issues. I [created r/WeeklyThing](https://www.thingelstad.com/2022/10/30/i-decided-to.html) in October 2022, and in September 2023 I opened the [Weekly Thing Forum](https://www.thingelstad.com/2023/09/22/introducing-weekly-thing.html) on Ponder, which closed when Ponder shut down in November 2025 ([Farewell Ponder and Weekly Thing Forum](https://www.thingelstad.com/2025/11/17/farewell-weekly-thing-forum-and.html)). Discussion moved back to the subreddit ([Weekly Thing 334](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/334/)).

Since November 2024, readers can become [Supporting Members](https://www.thingelstad.com/2024/11/17/weekly-thing-supporting.html). All of that money goes to one digital non-profit each year: Creative Commons first, then the Electronic Frontier Foundation, which [received $1,164.92](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/347/) in May 2026, and now [Signal](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/350/).

On February 25, 2025, I [made a custom GPT](https://www.thingelstad.com/2025/02/25/weekly-thing-gpt.html) that anyone with a ChatGPT account could use, “loaded with all 310 issues of the Weekly Thing published so far.” I suggested questions such as “What is the Weekly Thing view on social media?”, “What is worse, Facebook or TikTok?”, and “Show me a list of articles on X along with the issue they were in,” and announced it in [Weekly Thing 311](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/311/).

It had limits. In March 2025 I showed it [answering wrongly](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/313/) when asked which issue the Fortune first appeared in. Fourteen months later I launched Thingy, which searches the archive and cites its sources, and compared the two in [Weekly Thing 347](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/347/): the GPT “was grade school level. Thingy is much smarter!” The GPT’s link no longer works.

things.summary: Four AI agents on Discord, Eddy, Linky, Marky and Patty, that helped me edit, research, promote and fund the Weekly Thing in 2026.

things.body:
After nine years of Weekly Things assembled with Shortcuts, I wanted help that did not wait for me. The old workflow “only runs when I engage with it. It is also brittle and ‘one way’.” In May 2026 I introduced [the Weekly Thing Team](https://www.thingelstad.com/2026/05/12/the-weekly-thing-team.html), “the genesis of my Workshop,” four agents on Discord, each with the whole Weekly Thing archive as a tool:

- **Eddy**, the editor, assembled a working draft of the current issue every day and reviewed it.
- **Linky**, the researcher, scouted the links I flagged. When I replied with my commentary, Linky synced it back to Pinboard.
- **Marky** worked on bringing the newest issue to new readers.
- **Patty** ran the Supporting Membership calls to action, and was the only agent whose drafts appeared in an issue.

“My words are mine!” I wrote; the agents were a support team, not writers. [Weekly Thing 349](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/349/), sent on May 23, 2026, was the first issue made start to finish in the Workshop, “by far the biggest change I’ve ever made to the Weekly Thing automation.” Over the summer, as I put it in [Weekly Thing 350](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/350/), work on an Agent Studio “kind of blew up my own publishing process.” That issue was the first made in WT Builder, which has made every issue since.

things.title: WikiApiary
things.summary: A Semantic MediaWiki site that tracks thousands of MediaWiki wikis, their software, extensions, and editing activity.

observation.description: Celery-based task workers for collecting and updating data on WikiApiary.
The WikiApiary Wikibots

connections.label: is skinned with
connections.detail: WikiApiary’s distinctive look came from the Foreground skin, which I worked on for WikiApiary.

things.body:
WikiApiary is “a wiki to track other wikis.” Once a MediaWiki site is registered, a set of bots collects its software versions, extensions, skins, and editing statistics, and the wiki keeps the history so it can be charted and queried. It is built with MediaWiki and Semantic MediaWiki. I started it as a holiday-break project in 2012; [MediaWiki.org](https://www.mediawiki.org/wiki/WikiApiary) dates it to December 21, 2012. On [Open Loop #7](https://www.thingelstad.com/projects/open-loop/7-turtle-turtle-turtle/) in January 2013 I said I built it “in about three days,” after Semantic Result Formats’ charts showed me I could graph wiki statistics, and that Garrick van Buren came up with the name: the MediaWiki logo is a sunflower, the bots are like bees, and a collection of hives is an apiary.

After its first year it was collecting from 9,555 active wikis and had stored more than 1.8 billion statistics samples, with over 3.3 million property values of its own ([One Year for WikiApiary](https://www.thingelstad.com/2013/12/22/one-year-for.html)). I called it the first project I started that grew a real community around it. Karsten Hoffmeyer helped administer it, Mark Hershberger explored ways for wikis to register themselves, Paul DeCoursey rewrote the chart code, and Federico Leva linked MediaWiki.org’s extension pages to their WikiApiary pages, which brought much of its traffic.

When I decided I was done with it, others took it on. Mark Hershberger wrote in April 2017 that he had “[inherited the site from Jamie Thingelstad](https://lists.wikimedia.org/hyperkitty/list/wikiapiary@lists.wikimedia.org/message/HRNMPDZBNH5DWCWEFWMKLJAACDQDOAPY/).” That October, Hershberger and his son Basil began [moving it from the old Linode servers to Wikimedia Cloud Services](https://lists.wikimedia.org/hyperkitty/list/wikiapiary@lists.wikimedia.org/message/R7TRLEB73RKAGGA22VE3JAVW3YZOQSMF/). At its size the wiki has struggled with database timeouts: it [came back online](https://lists.wikimedia.org/hyperkitty/list/wikiapiary@lists.wikimedia.org/message/7HK7OPHOID3ZLCYSZTNPXDPG7MHTXGMV/) in March 2023 after an upgrade to MediaWiki 1.39, was [in write-only mode](https://lists.wikimedia.org/hyperkitty/list/wikiapiary@lists.wikimedia.org/message/AMVVOP72ONA2YI7XJ7KV6O3K42BBBES4/) by that September, and MediaWiki.org marked it not operational in February 2025.

In March 2026 Brian Wolff [got the site serving pages again](https://lists.wikimedia.org/hyperkitty/list/wikiapiary@lists.wikimedia.org/message/W5UMMJTSPGP7ZFT2NPTLCFHVVUXOLIOO/), with the update bots still off, and in May 2026 Hershberger announced from the Wikimedia Hackathon that WikiApiary and its bots [were moving to a Kubernetes cluster](https://lists.wikimedia.org/hyperkitty/list/wikiapiary@lists.wikimedia.org/message/DCSXARUPRRYZO4XKTTJXYIDM3T5AAGIV/) so it could start crawling wikis again.

things.title: Wikinosh
things.summary: A Semantic MediaWiki site of nutrition facts for more than 20,000 foods, with a Twitter bot and an offline app.

connections.label: used
connections.detail: WikiApiary listed Numbers2Words 0.0.1 among Wikinosh’s extensions, and the main page spelled out its food counts.

things.body:
Wikinosh was a wiki of nutrition facts. Each food had a page with a nutrition label (serving size, calories, fat, sodium, carbohydrates, and protein) stored as Semantic MediaWiki properties, and foods were grouped into categories such as Baby Foods, Beverages, and Spices and Herbs. The Internet Archive first captured it in [December 2011](https://web.archive.org/web/20111205190345/http://wikinosh.com/wiki/Main_Page) with 13,753 food records; by [mid-2012](https://web.archive.org/web/20120630194132/http://wikinosh.com/wiki/Main_Page) it listed 21,550. In January 2013 [WikiApiary](https://web.archive.org/web/20130103025340/http://wikiapiary.com/wiki/Wikinosh) counted 20,433 articles and 981,167 property values on it.

In [Open Loop #2](https://www.thingelstad.com/projects/open-loop/2-what-am-i-editing-anyway/) in June 2012, I described the food wiki I had “kind of in alpha” and how turning on Wikimedia Commons let a page show a photo of a banana just by naming the file. In July 2013 I worked with Yaron Koren to put Wikinosh’s data into Koren’s Miga app for offline, mobile access, and wrote up the Semantic MediaWiki limits I hit exporting more than 20,000 items ([Paging Large Datasets in Semantic MediaWiki](https://www.thingelstad.com/2013/07/30/paging-large-datasets.html)).

The @Wikinosh Twitter account posted a random food from its 28,000-plus entries every six hours; in November 2013 one of those posts, about trout, drew an IRC-style trout slap from another bot ([Slapped with a Large Trout](https://www.thingelstad.com/2013/11/04/slapped-with-a.html)). The last Internet Archive capture of the wiki is from April 2014, and by November 2014 I listed @Wikinosh among the Twitter accounts I had deleted ([Twitter Spam #NFL](https://www.thingelstad.com/2014/11/28/twitter-spam-nfl.html)).

things.body:
WT Builder is the authoring app for the Weekly Thing. I started building it with Claude in July 2026 to replace the Weekly Thing Workshop, the team of Discord agents that had itself taken over in May 2026 from the Shortcuts workflow I had used for nine years. It combines what I write for an issue with links and posts pulled from Pinboard and Micro.blog. The issue stays structured until it is sent, and then WT Builder renders three different editions: the website, the Buttondown email, and the audio edition for the podcast. The [README](https://github.com/jthingelstad/wt-builder) says it is narrow on purpose: “one editor, one current issue, one newsletter.”

[Weekly Thing 350](https://www.thingelstad.com/2026/09/20/i-just-published-weekly-thing.html), sent on September 20, 2026, was the first issue made in it. I had Claude watch me use it that first time and fix problems as they came up. The next day we [reworked the audio edition](https://www.thingelstad.com/2026/09/21/weekly-thing-podcast-improvements.html), with better pauses, section announcements, and pronunciation, plus links in the episode descriptions. In October I [added an MCP server](https://www.thingelstad.com/2026/10/03/my-newest-mcp-experiment-was.html) so Claude could follow along as I wrote and point out typos and grammar.

On October 11, 2026, WT Builder also [took over the Another Thing podcast](https://github.com/jthingelstad/wt-builder/commit/bea76c7ef4fc79a878072feebf694ce18ad217ea) from the retired Another Thing Builder. The Shortcuts workflow is kept as a fallback.

things.body:
For a few years I had wondered about a book version of the Weekly Thing, something like an almanac. I [started it over Christmas 2025](https://www.thingelstad.com/2026/01/19/i-just-finished-up-this.html) and [published it](https://www.thingelstad.com/2026/01/20/i-made-a-book-yearly.html) on January 20, 2026, as _Yearly Thing 2025: Agents, Attention, Artifacts_. It gathers all 324 links I commented on across 31 issues in 2025 into ten topic chapters, from The AI Revolution to Tools, Productivity and Delights, with an Introduction, a Weekly Thing Index, and an Afterword. The eBook keeps every hyperlink. The paperback lists the issue each item came from, with QR codes that lead to the Weekly Thing Index.

“I made the Yearly Thing with Claude Code,” I wrote in [Weekly Thing 339](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/339/), and I laid out the book in Vellum. The [paperback is $30 on Lulu](https://www.lulu.com/shop/jamie-thingelstad/yearly-thing-2025/paperback/product-84w66ey.html), and the first print copies [arrived on January 27](https://www.thingelstad.com/2026/01/27/the-print-copies-of-the.html). The [eBook is $20 on Gumroad](https://jthingelstad.gumroad.com/l/yearly-thing-2025). Anyone who bought it in the first two months got a [Yearly Thing 2025 POAP](https://poap.gallery/drops/223594). All proceeds go to the Weekly Thing Supporting Membership program, and the book’s sales were part of the [$1,164.92 given to the Electronic Frontier Foundation](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/347/) in May 2026.

things.summary: A website that writes your age as a software version, decades.years.days, with a Work Edition for job tenure.

story.introduction: A different way to count the days.

The related Release Notes product adds daily email and a personal journal. It has its own server and storage.
questions: How does the version number work?
How is Release Notes related?

things.body:
In February 2018 I wrote [Your Version Number](https://www.thingelstad.com/2018/02/24/your-version-number.html), building on a habit of my friend David Hussman, who gave his age as a version number. I mapped it to semantic versioning: decades are the major version, years into the decade the minor, and days since the last birthday the patch. I was v4.6.52 that day, and I made a Workflow script to show the versions of people in my address book. David died that August; the [site’s About page](https://yourversionnumber.com/about/) says the arithmetic is his.

After a year of seeing my version through a [shortcut on my phone](https://www.thingelstad.com/2025/02/25/jamie.html), I made it a website with Claude Code in May 2026, first shared in [Weekly Thing 346](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/346/) on 2026-05-03 and then in [a launch post](https://www.thingelstad.com/2026/05/06/your-version-number-the-website.html). Add one or more birthdays, pick one of the themes, and the page shows each version, counting up at midnight. Everything is held in the URL, so a view can be bookmarked, set as a home page, or sent to someone, with no account. Cards with a signed note work the same way.

The Work Edition applies the same idea to a job: completed years of tenure, the quarter of the current tenure year, and weekdays into that quarter, with a build number that counts every business day, and work themes such as a board update. In October 2026 the idea grew into [Release Notes](https://notes.yourversionnumber.com/), a daily email of the day’s version with a journal attached.
